minor: "Call it a lake, and Iran could claim 20 percent, not about 13": 20 percent is Iran's own proposal of equal shares. A lake regime does not automatically give Iran 20 percent, so attribute it aloud here too ("Iran argues a lake means 20 percent").

"Its surface sits about 28 metres below the level of the world's oceans": the level varies year to year (the source notes this). "About" covers it, but "roughly" or "in recent decades" would be safer.
"Iran's parliament has not ratified the convention": the source trail only runs through 2024. Re-check ratification status before publishing on 24 Nov 2026.

"The oil below is split like a sea" (and the outro echo) slightly overstates. Article 8 only leaves the seabed to neighbours' agreements, and the south still has no accepted line. "Is to be split by neighbours' deals, like a sea" is more exact.
"Leaving Persia no navy on its own coast" goes slightly beyond Article V, which gave Russia alone the right to keep warships. Persia was barred from them, not from all vessels.
The 1940 line "a Soviet and Iranian sea" comes from an exchange of letters attached to the treaty. "A 1940 treaty" is acceptable, but "a 1940 exchange of letters" is more exact.
"A map of the Gulistan village in the Caucasus": Gulistan lay in Karabakh. Naming the region ("in Karabakh") would be more precise than "a village in the Caucasus".
The 2015 Syria missile strike is tangential to the sea-or-lake question. It only supports the no-outside-forces rule, so one more clause linking it to Article 3 would help.
"Iran's coast is short and curves inward" has no listed source. It is a geographic description, not a figure, but it should carry a Britannica or map citation.

shots.vo: The Caspian sits where Europe meets Asia, and it is the largest inland body of water on Earth.
It covers about 371,000 square kilometres, a little more than the whole of Germany.
Five countries share its coast: Russia and Kazakhstan in the north, Turkmenistan east, Iran south, Azerbaijan west.
In the south, the floor drops to about 1,025 metres, deep enough to stack three Eiffel Towers.
The north is a different world: it averages about five metres deep, and it freezes in winter.
The Volga brings in about four fifths of its water, and no river carries any of it to an ocean.
Its surface sits about 28 metres below the level of the world's oceans, closed in on every side.

The same 2013 US estimate counted 292 trillion cubic feet of gas around the basin, beside the oil.

In the south, between Iran, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan, there is still no seabed line all sides accept.
To see why, go back two hundred years, to a war Persia lost in the mountains to the west.

But nobody drew a line across the water, because for a century the water itself was not the prize.
Then the oil boom came. By 1900, Baku produced about half of all the world's crude oil.

shots.vo: A 1940 treaty went further and called the Caspian a Soviet and Iranian sea, shared by two states.

quote.who: Soviet-Iranian Treaty of Commerce and Navigation

shots.vo: Each side kept a fishing zone of ten nautical miles from its coast, and the rest, by the treaty's wording, was open to both.
In 1970, Moscow's oil ministry split the Soviet part of the seabed into sectors for four Soviet republics.
Its southern edge was a straight line from Astara to Hasankuli, a line Iran says it never accepted.
Then, in December 1991, the Soviet Union broke apart, and two Caspian countries became five.
Every treaty until then had been written for two countries, and not one of them divided the seabed.
On 20 September 1994, Azerbaijan signed what it called the Contract of the Century with foreign oil companies.

shots.vo: Russia protested, arguing the Caspian's riches belonged to all its coastal states until they agreed otherwise.
Four years later, Russia and Kazakhstan changed course and split their northern seabed with a modified median line.
A modified median line runs halfway between two coasts, then bends where a deal over a field says so.
Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan followed in 2001, Russia and Azerbaijan in 2002, and the three joined their lines in 2003.
The north was settled by handshakes, but in the south, one summer day in 2001 showed how fragile things were.
On 23 July 2001, an Iranian warship ordered a BP survey ship to leave a field Azerbaijan calls Alov.

shots.vo: Iran calls the same field Alborz and says it lies in its waters, and BP stopped work there.
Under a median line, Reuters and Al Jazeera give Iran about 13 percent of the seabed, though figures range from 11 to 14.
Iran has argued for 20 percent, an equal fifth for each of the five coastal countries.
Iran's coast is short and curves inward, so halfway lines leave its corner of the seabed small.
Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Russia point to the rule used in most of the world's seas: divide from each coast.
Their case, at its strongest: median lines split the North Sea's oil, so why treat the Caspian differently?
Iran's case, at its strongest: two treaties made this a shared sea, so nobody should carve it up alone.
On 12 August 2018, after more than two decades of talks, the five presidents met in Aktau, Kazakhstan.
There they signed the Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, the first such deal all five signed.

headline.text: Five Caspian states sign status convention in Aktau

shots.vo: Each country gets 15 nautical miles of territorial water, plus a 10-mile fishing zone beyond that.
The middle stays common water, open to ships of all five flags, much as a shared lake would be.
But the seabed, where the oil lies, is left for neighbours to divide by agreements between themselves.
So ships on top are shared like a lake, and the oil below is split like a sea.

shots.vo: The treaty adds one more rule: no armed forces from outside the five may sail on the Caspian.
On 7 October 2015, Russia's Caspian Flotilla fired cruise missiles across Iran and Iraq at targets in Syria, Reuters reported.
Russia's defence ministry said 26 missiles were launched that day, from ships in this landlocked water.

shots.vo: Iran's parliament has not ratified the convention, and it only takes force once all five have done so.
In January 2021, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan agreed to develop together a field they had both claimed.
Baku called it Kapaz, Ashgabat called it Serdar, and now both call it Dostluk, meaning friendship.

shots.vo: That deal revived an old plan: a gas pipeline of about 300 kilometres from Turkmenbashi to Baku.
From Baku, the gas could join pipes through Georgia and Turkey to southern Europe, without crossing Russia.
The 2018 convention says a pipeline needs only the countries whose seabed sectors it crosses, plus environmental standards.

shots.vo: Russia and Iran have both raised environmental objections; Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan say the project can meet the rules.
So the treaty drew some lines on paper. But the water itself is now moving the coast.
First scenario: Iran ratifies, then agrees seabed lines with Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan, closing the last gaps.
Fields like Alov would then have an agreed owner, and drilling in the deep south could finally begin.

shots.vo: Iran's government said in 2018 that seabed limits still need a separate agreement, and that is where talks stand.
Second scenario: the water keeps falling. A 2020 study projected a drop of 9 to 18 metres by 2100.
The authors tied it mainly to warming, which lifts evaporation faster than the rivers can refill the basin.

Kazakhstan's government already reports the water dropping along its coast.

shots.vo: Third scenario: the pipeline gets built, and Turkmen gas reaches Europe across this seabed instead of through Russia.
Europe would gain a gas source in Central Asia, and the seabed between Turkmenbashi and Baku would carry it.
Or the plan stays on paper, as it has since the late 1990s, and Turkmen gas keeps flowing east to China.
So in the end, which is it: a sea, or a lake?

shots.vo: The answer: on the surface, the Caspian works like a lake; underneath, its oil is split like a sea.
The treaty left the word out, and so the question of who owns the oil in the south is still open.
